## Verdict: The claim is false — current evidence does not support it

**Origin of the claim:** In March 2020, French Health Minister Olivier Véran tweeted that NSAIDs like ibuprofen could "aggravate" COVID-19 infection, urging paracetamol instead. This was based on speculative concerns—not data—that NSAIDs might upregulate ACE2 receptors (the entry point the virus uses into cells) and could mask fever, potentially delaying diagnosis (https://www.nytimes.com/2020/03/17/health/coronavirus-ibuprofen.html).

**What the evidence actually shows:**
- The WHO reviewed available data and found "no evidence" that ibuprofen use worsens COVID-19 outcomes, a position echoed by Health Canada and other national health agencies (https://www.cbc.ca/news/health/ibuprofen-covid-19-novel-coronavirus-1.5501496).
- Multiple health authorities investigating the claim (WHO, UK's MHRA, US FDA) explicitly stated they were "not aware of reports of any negative effects of ibuprofen, beyond the usual known side effects" specific to COVID-19 (https://www.news4jax.com/health/2020/03/20/health-agencies-no-evidence-ibuprofen-worsens-coronavirus/).
- Investigative reporting (NPR, Wired) found the scare was rooted in a single hypothesis-generating letter in *The Lancet Respiratory Medicine* about ACE2 receptors—theoretical reasoning, not clinical evidence. Experts called the French guidance "baffling," noting no statistical relationship between ibuprofen use and worse outcomes had ever been demonstrated (https://www.npr.org/sections/health-shots/2020/03/18/818026613/advice-from-france-to-avoid-ibuprofen-for-covid-19-leaves-experts-baffled; https://www.wired.com/story/the-ibuprofen-debate-reveals-the-danger-of-covid-19-rumors/).

**Bottom line:** The alarm was driven by mechanistic speculation and a single official's tweet, not clinical data. Health authorities worldwide subsequently confirmed there is no evidence ibuprofen worsens COVID-19, and it remains an approved option for symptom relief. As with any NSAID, standard precautions (e.g., kidney disease, GI issues) still apply, but COVID-19-specific danger is not substantiated.
